'''Peter B. Dervan''' (born June 28, 1945) is the Bren Professor of [[Chemistry]] at the [[California Institute of Technology]]. The primary focus of his research is the development and study of small organic molecules that can sequence-specifically recognize [[DNA]].<ref name="Dervan">{{cite journal|last1=Dervan1986|first1=P.B.|title=Design of sequence-specific-DNA-binding molecules|journal=Science|date=1986|volume=232|issue=4749|pages=464–471|pmid=2421408|doi=10.1126/science.2421408|bibcode=1986Sci...232..464D}}</ref><ref name="Southwestern">{{cite news|title=Caltech Chemist Peter Dervan to Deliver Lecture|url=http://www.southwestern.edu/live/news/10473-caltech-chemist-peter-dervan-to-deliver-lecture|access-date=15 June 2017|work=Southwestern Newsroom|quote=“Professor Dervan is an internationally renowned chemist and recognized pioneer in chemical biology."}}</ref> The most important of these small molecules are [[pyrrole–imidazole polyamides]].<ref name="Tetrahedron"/>
Dervan is credited with influencing "the course of research in organic chemistry through his studies at the interface of chemistry and biology" as a result of his work on "the chemical principles involved in sequence-specific recognition of double helical DNA".<ref name="Avery"/>
He is the recipient of many awards, including the [[National Medal of Science]] (2006).<ref name="Mantell"/><ref name="NAS"/>

==Early life and education==
Peter B. Dervan was born on June 28, 1945, in Boston, Massachusetts. He grew up in a family of six in [[Dorchester, Boston|Dorchester]], a working-class suburb of Boston.<ref name="Priestley address">{{cite magazine |last1=Dervan |first1=Peter B. |title=Priestley Medal address 2022: Skydiving into the interface of chemistry and biology |magazine=[[Chemical & Engineering News]] |date=March 20, 2022 |volume=100 |issue=10 |url=https://cen.acs.org/biological-chemistry/dna/Priestley-Medal-address-2022-Skydiving-into-the-interface-of-chemistry-and-biology/100/i10 |access-date=4 April 2023}}</ref> Dervan attended [[Boston College High School]] and received his B.S. degree from [[Boston College]] in 1967,<ref name="Priestley address"/><ref name="Illinois"/> where professor Francis Bennett sparked his interest in organic chemistry.<ref name="Mantell"/> He began graduate studies at the [[University of Wisconsin]] then moved with [[Jerome A. Berson]]'s research group to [[Yale University]] where he completed his graduate research in physical organic chemistry,<ref name="Wohl"/> studying ways in which chemical bonds are created and broken apart.<ref name="Mantell"/> He received his [[Ph.D.]] degree from [[Yale University]] in 1972, for ''The Stereochemistry of the Thermal Rearrangements of Trans-1,2-Dialkenylcyclobutanes and Cis-1,2-Dialkenylcyclobutanes''.<ref name="Tree">{{cite web|title=Peter B. Dervan|url=https://academictree.org/chemistry/peopleinfo.php?pid=52764|website=Chemistry Tree|access-date=14 June 2017}}</ref><ref name="thesis-dervan-1973">{{cite thesis |title=The stereochemistry of the thermal rearrangements of trans- and cis-1,2-dialkenylcyclobutanes |date=1973 |publisher=[[Yale University]] |degree=Ph.D. |last=Dervan |first=Peter Brendan |oclc=418780449 |id={{ProQuest|47891156}}}}</ref> He then became an NIH postdoctoral fellow at [[Stanford University|Stanford]], working with [[Eugene van Tamelen]].<ref name="Illinois">{{cite web|title=Carl Shipp Marvel Lecturer 2002–03 – Peter B. Dervan|url=http://www.chemistry.illinois.edu/events/lectures/CS_Marvel_Lecture_Series_in_Organic_Chemistry/Peter_Dervan.html|website=The Department of Chemistry at the University of Illinois|access-date=14 June 2017|archive-date=15 March 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220315225650/https://chemistry.illinois.edu/events/lectures/CS_Marvel_Lecture_Series_in_Organic_Chemistry/Peter_Dervan.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Career==
[[File:Peter Dervan 1986.png|thumb|left|Dervan in 1986]]

Dervan became an assistant professor of chemistry at [[California Institute of Technology|Caltech]] in 1973,<ref name="Illinois"/> joining [[John D. Roberts]], [[Robert G. Bergman]] and Robert Ellsworth Ireland in the organic chemistry group.<ref name="Tetrahedron"/> He became an associate professor in 1979, and professor in 1982. He was appointed as the first Bren Professor of [[Chemistry]] in 1988.<ref name="ancham">{{cite journal|title=For Your Information|journal=Analytical Chemistry|date=30 May 2012|volume=60|issue=6|pages=379A|doi=10.1021/ac00157a715}}</ref><ref name="Illinois"/> He served as Chair of Caltech's Division of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering from 1994 to 1999.<ref name="Yale"/> Dervan has published more than 360 papers and taught hundreds of students.<ref name="Wohl"/>

Dervan is a member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] (1986),<ref name="NAS1986">{{cite journal|title=Chemists elected to National Academy of Sciences|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=5 May 1986|volume=64|issue=18|pages=6|doi=10.1021/cen-v064n018.p006a}}</ref> 
the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] (1987),<ref>{{cite journal|title=NEWS|journal=Analytical Chemistry|date=September 1988|volume=60|issue=18|pages=1029A|doi=10.1021/ac00169a711}}</ref> and 
the [[American Philosophical Society]] (2002).<ref name="APS2002">{{cite web|title=Peter B. Dervan|url=http://www.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=Peter+Dervan&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced|website=American Philosophical Society|access-date=14 June 2017}}</ref> 
He is an elected member of the [[French Academy of Sciences]] (2000)<ref name="France">{{cite web|title=Peter Dervan|url=http://www.academie-sciences.fr/en/Liste-des-membres-de-l-Academie-des-sciences-/-D/peter-dervan.html|website=Institute de France Académie des Sciences|access-date=14 June 2017}}</ref> 
and the [[Academy of Sciences Leopoldina|Deutsche Akademie der Naturforscher Leopoldina]] (2004– ).<ref name="Schnitzer-Ungefug">{{cite news|last1=Schnitzer-Ungefug|first1=Jutta|title=Deutsche Akademie der Naturforscher Leopoldina wählt neue Mitglieder Prof|url=https://idw-online.de/de/news84545|access-date=14 June 2017|work=Informationsdienst Wissenschaft|date=December 8, 2004}}</ref>

==Research==
While teaching a class at Caltech in Advanced Organic Chemistry, Dervan came to a realization that would guide his future career: rather than working to "close" a classic problem that had been previously defined, he would seek to define and "open" a new research area that could be studied for many years.<ref name="Tetrahedron"/>  
The problem he chose was molecular recognition in biological systems.<ref name="Mantell"/>  At the time, DNA sequencing was in its infancy and the human genome project was undreamt of. Dervan chose to apply ideas from synthetic chemistry to biology and the study of DNA, creating novel binding molecules to be used for DNA recognition.<ref name="Tetrahedron"/>

By studying weak intermolecular interactions and creating novel synthetic molecules specific to particular DNA sequences, Dervan has been able to explore the complex biological systems underlying DNA's structure and function.<ref name="Wohl"/>  A human cell contains approximately 20,000 genes, whose expression is controlled by the binding of protein transcription factors in the promoter region of each gene.<ref name="Tetrahedron"/> Through pioneering work in DNA recognition,<ref name="Wohl"/> Dervan has determined many of the chemical principles underlying sequence-specific recognition of DNA,<ref name="Tetrahedron"/> and enabled researchers to better understand the mechanism of action of many anti-tumor, anti-viral and anti-biotic drugs.<ref name="ancham"/>

Dervan determined that small molecules could be synthesized and used to selectively bind DNA at the transcription factor/DNA interface, effectively rewriting the biological codes controlling transcription by acting on the promoters of selected genes.<ref name="Mantell"/> 
The creation of synthetic small molecules with affinities and sequence specificities for predetermined DNA sequences makes it possible to design cell-permeable molecules for the regulation of gene expression.<ref name="Illinois"/>
The use of small molecules to regulate gene expression in living cells has possible application to human medicine.<ref name="Tetrahedron"/><ref name="Edelson">{{cite journal|last1=Dervan|first1=Peter B|last2=Edelson|first2=Benjamin S|title=Recognition of the DNA minor groove by pyrrole-imidazole polyamides|journal=Current Opinion in Structural Biology|date=June 2003|volume=13|issue=3|pages=284–299|doi=10.1016/S0959-440X(03)00081-2|pmid=12831879}}</ref>

The most important of these small molecules are pyrrole–imidazole polyamides.<ref name="Edelson"/><ref name="Recognition">{{cite journal|last1=Dervan|first1=PB|last2=Edelson|first2=BS|title=Recognition of the DNA minor groove by pyrrole-imidazole polyamides.|journal=Current Opinion in Structural Biology|date=June 2003|volume=13|issue=3|pages=284–99|pmid=12831879|doi=10.1016/s0959-440x(03)00081-2}}</ref> Dervan's lab has identified pairing rules to control the DNA sequence specificity of minor-groove binding polyamides that contain the aromatic ring amino acids hydroxypyrrole (Hp), imidazole (Im), and pyrrole (Py).<ref name="Swalley">{{cite journal|last1=Swalley|first1=Susanne E.|last2=Baird|first2=Eldon E.|last3=Dervan|first3=Peter B.|title=A Pyrrole-Imidazole Polyamide Motif for Recognition of Eleven Base Pair Sequences in the Minor Groove of DNA|journal=Chemistry – A European Journal|date=October 1997|volume=3|issue=10|pages=1600–1607|doi=10.1002/chem.19970031009 |bibcode=1997ChEuJ...3.1600S }}</ref><ref name="Edelson"/><ref name="White">{{cite journal|last1=White|first1=Sarah|last2=Baird|first2=Eldon E.|last3=Dervan|first3=Peter B.|title=On the pairing rules for recognition in the minor groove of DNA by pyrrole-imidazole polyamides|journal=Chemistry & Biology|date=August 1997|volume=4|issue=8|pages=569–578|doi=10.1016/S1074-5521(97)90243-X|pmid=9281524|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Awards==
Dervan has received a number of awards for both research and teaching,<ref name="Illinois"/> including those listed below.  He was awarded the 2006 [[National Medal of Science]] in 2007 from President George Bush at the White House for “his fundamental research contributions at the interface of organic chemistry and biology” as well as contributions to education and industry.<ref name="NAS">{{cite web |url=https://www.nsf.gov/news/news_summ.jsp?cntn_id=109741 |title=2006 National Medal of Science Winners |access-date=2009-02-08 |publisher=United States Government |archive-date=2022-03-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220309084916/https://www.nsf.gov/news/news_summ.jsp?cntn_id=109741 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>[https://www.nsf.gov/od/nms/recip_details.cfm?recip_id=5300000000437 National Science Foundation – The President's National Medal of Science]</ref><ref name="Mantell">{{cite news|last1=Mantell|first1=Suzanne|title=A day at the races|url=http://bcm.bc.edu/issues/spring_2008/works/a-day-at-the-races.html|access-date=14 June 2017|work=Boston College Magazine|archive-date=10 November 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191110060110/http://bcm.bc.edu/issues/spring_2008/works/a-day-at-the-races.html/|url-status=dead}}</ref> A minor planet has been named in his honor, [[4314 Dervan]].<ref name="Schmadel">{{cite book|last1=Schmadel|first1=Lutz|title=Dictionary of Minor Planet Names: Addendum to 6th Edition: 2012–2014|date=2014|publisher=Springer|location=New York|page=48|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dzBsCQAAQBAJ&pg=PA48|access-date=14 June 2017|isbn=9783319176772}}</ref>

==Personal==
In 1990, Dervan married [[Jacqueline Barton]], a fellow chemist and professor at [[Caltech]]. He has a son, Andrew, from a previous marriage, and a daughter, Elizabeth, from his marriage with Barton.<ref name=Priestley2015>{{cite journal|title=Meet Jacqueline K. Barton, 2015 Priestley Medalist|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=Mar 23, 2015|volume=93|issue=12|url=http://cen.acs.org/articles/93/i12/Meet-Jaqueline-K-Barton-2015.html|access-date=2 April 2015}}</ref><ref name="Yale"/> All four hold degrees from Yale University.<ref name="Wohl">{{cite news|last1=Wohl|first1=Shirlee|title=Peter Dervan, GRD '72|url=http://www.yalescientific.org/2011/11/peter-dervan-grd-72/|access-date=14 June 2017|work=Yale Scientific|date=November 16, 2011}}</ref>
